column1: # ---- 04-compliance/T0 ----
L1, L2, L3 and L5 are pure functions of their declared contract inputs.
Every seam payload is an immutable, serialisable, content-addressed value.
Every run is reproducible from a manifest.
Every seam can be recorded: a run writes C1 through C5 payloads to disk, and a recorded seam is a test fixture rather than a log line.

Every layer can be replayed in isolation: Valuation against a recorded C1 stream with no Belief store, no network and no clock; the Planner against a recorded C2 stream with no Valuation present; Settlement against a recorded C4 stream with no knowledge of what was intended.
Every comparison is exact, because two runs of the same manifest produce byte-identical artefacts, so whether a change altered behaviour is a hash comparison rather than a judgement call.
Removing recordability, isolated replay or exactness degrades every level above T1 into smoke tests.
Hidden state in L2 or L3 breaks isolated replay.
A wall-clock read or an unordered iteration breaks exactness of comparison.
A contract carrying an object reference breaks seam recordability.
Purity, no-clock-read and no-object-reference are hard failures rather than style rules because the compliance architecture rests on them.
Replaying a recorded C1 stream against L2 alone proves valuation is a function of belief.
Replaying a recorded C2 stream against L3 alone proves the plan is a function of primitives.
Replaying recorded C3 and C4 streams against L5 alone proves settlement is a function of outcome.
Replaying C1 through C5 plus the manifest over the whole tick proves the golden hash and the Merkle chain.
T0 answers whether a view or component computes what its own spec says, on its own.
T1 answers whether what crosses a seam satisfies the contract in schema, units, ranges, no-NaN and version, and whether two solver backends agree.
T2 answers whether the layer obeys the relations that must hold for every input, including inputs nobody wrote a fixture for.
T3 answers whether the run is reproducible, the artefact chain intact, and the tick acyclic.
T4 answers whether the fitted fill, activation and quoting models match observed reality.
T5 answers how much value the shipped tier gives up against the oracle and at what solve cost.
T6 answers whether the engine can be made to peek, to accept garbage, or to use an expired artefact.
The seven levels are ordered by what they need in place rather than by importance.
T2 requires T1, because a payload that fails schema cannot be property-tested meaningfully.
T5 and T6 both require T3, because without determinism a measured difference proves nothing.

T0's scope is one view, one composer stage, one calendar function or one term shape, with no I/O and no solver, budgeted at 60 seconds for the whole suite, blocking a commit on failure, owned by the layer owner.

T1's scope is each seam payload C1 to C5 plus the StateSnapshot, the MarketCalendar artefact, and backend agreement on one model, budgeted at 3 minutes, blocking a merge, owned by the contracts owner.
T2's scope is per layer and per seam with generated inputs and bounded shrinking, budgeted at 15 minutes in CI with an extended nightly corpus, blocking a merge, owned by the layer owner.

T3's scope is the whole tick then the whole run, with golden hashes over a canonical 7-day window in CI and full history nightly, budgeted at 8 minutes in CI and 3 hours nightly, blocking a merge on an unexplained hash change and paging the on-call on nightly failure, owned by the platform owner.

T4's scope is the fill model, activation model and quoting policy against the simulator, run nightly within 2 hours, raising an alert and a calibration ticket and blocking a release if drift exceeds the published band, owned by the quant and calibration owner.
T5's scope is Tiers 1, 2 and 3 on a holdout backtest plus scaling curves in S and in breakpoint count, run overnight per release, blocking a release, owned by the optimisation owner.

T6's scope is the whole run under adversarial mutation — poisoned future facts, poisoned config, fuzzed payloads, tampered ledger, expired artefacts — run reduced nightly and full per release, blocking a release, with a lookahead divergence a stop-ship, owned by the risk and audit owner.
The runtime budgets are targets for the CI configuration, which is the deterministic single-threaded solver configuration.
Production runs with more threads and a different manifest, and its throughput is not a test budget.
The pre-commit hook runs T0 and T1 in full, a fast fixed-seed subset of T2, and a one-tick golden smoke of T3.
Pull request CI runs T0 and T1 in full, T2 in full with a fixed seed, and a 7-day golden window of T3.
The nightly run covers T0 and T1 in full, an extended rotating-seed T2 corpus, full-history T3 with the acyclicity audit, full T4, T5 scaling curves only, and reduced T6.
The pre-release run covers T0 through T3 in full, T4 in full with drift review, and T5 and T6 in full.
The post-deploy canary runs full T1 because production validation is always on, a live hash of the production manifest for T3, live drift monitors for T4, and live gap telemetry for T5.
The pre-commit and PR runs use a fixed seed so a failure is reproducible by the author on the first attempt.
The nightly run rotates the seed and, on failure, writes the failing seed and the shrunk counterexample into the corpus as a permanent regression fixture.
A property test that found a bug once becomes a unit test forever.
Merging requires T0 green, with no exceptions and no per-PR waivers.
Merging requires T1 green for every seam, and a contract change additionally requires the version bump, the layer-design update and the conformance-test update in the same commit.
Merging requires T2 green.
Merging requires T3 golden hashes over the canonical window either unchanged or changed with a declared, reviewed baseline update naming the artefact that moved and the reason.
An undeclared hash change is a merge blocker even when the new numbers look better.
No new invariant severity downgrade may merge: lowering an invariant from HALT to warn is an architecture change and needs an ADR rather than a PR.
Releasing requires a T4 calibration report showing realised-versus-predicted fill rate by price band, product and time-to-gate within the published tolerance band, with reliability diagrams reviewed.
Releasing requires a T5 gap report for every tier that can run in production, since no tier ships without its gap measured against Tier 1.
The T5 gap report carries p50, p90, p99 and worst case, conditioned on regime, plus the Tier-1-to-perfect-foresight distance.
Releasing requires T5 scaling curves of objective and solve time versus scenario count and versus PWL breakpoint count, so the configured values are evidenced.
Releasing requires the full T6 adversarial suite green, including the lookahead poisoning audit at bit-identity.
Releasing requires the manifest pinned: code revision, config, MarketCalendar artefact, tzdata version, every model artefact, solver identity and determinism settings.
Going live requires a shadow period in which the engine runs against live data emitting intent that is recorded and not submitted, for a declared number of trading days.
T4 measures capture ratio and adverse selection over the shadow period.
Going live requires the reserve delivery shortfall invariant exercised in the simulator under the worst activation scenario in the ensemble, asserting HALT rather than under-delivery.

Going live requires a degradation drill forcing each of the five modes and confirming the transition, the hysteresis, the logged cause, and that peak protection and commitment feasibility survive every mode.
Going live requires an acknowledged operator runbook for HALT, because HALT requires human acknowledgement to resume and an unrehearsed first HALT is an outage.
Going live requires a recalibration plan for the fill model, because a simulator-calibrated model inherits the simulator's biases and the venue gap is a named risk from day one.
Validation stays on in production: the universal invariants are checked by the shared validator on both sides of every seam in every environment.
The cost of production validation is microseconds against a solve measured in milliseconds, and there is no flag that disables it.
A skipped test is a failing test: a skip requires a linked ticket and an expiry date, and an expired skip fails the build.
Every HALT-severity invariant has at least one test that provokes it.
An invariant nobody has ever seen fire is an invariant nobody knows is wired up.
T0's scope is a single pure function exercised through its own interface, with no solver, no file system and no recorded seam.

For each valuation view T0 asserts that Evaluate's output validates against the view's own PublishedSchema, that ClaimedEffects matches what the terms actually carry, and hand-computed values on a four-slot fixture.
For each composer stage T0 asserts the preconditions and postconditions of the stage table hold in isolation.
The curvature checker is tested on concave, convex, general and pathological breakpoint sets including ties and a two-point curve.
The epigraph builder is tested for the dominance constraints, the floor, the correct overSlots subset and the correct prorationFactor application.
The CivilCalendar is tested on the SlotId mapping to local date, local time and HLZF window on ordinary days and both DST days, and on 92, 96 and 100-slot civil days.
Typed quantities are tested for frame and unit conversions, and that illegal conversions do not compile, with compile-fail tests part of the suite.
The POI bridge is tested in isolation, both signs, with aux load present.
The SOC dynamics kernel is tested for one-way efficiency on each direction, split charge and discharge, and no free round trip.
Each of the five term shapes round-trips to binary and to JSON.
The fallback ladder is tested so that each rung is selected for the right input and the stopping rung is recorded.
T0 deliberately does not test interactions, and a unit test needing two views is a T2 property test on the composer.
The fixture corpus has three kinds of input, all versioned and content-addressed like any other artefact.
Hand-built micro-fixtures are written by hand over 4 to 16 slots with values computable on paper, used by T0 and as the minimal reproduction after T2 shrinking.
Recorded seams are captured from designated audit days of a real backtest and used by T1, T2 and T3 per-layer replay.
Generated inputs come from property-test generators constrained to produce contract-valid payloads and are used by T2 and T6 fuzzing.
Generators are written to satisfy the contract by construction, so a generator that emits NaN is testing T1 rather than T2 and the two must not be conflated.
Deliberately invalid payloads are a T6 concern where the assertion is clean rejection rather than correct computation.

The canonical window for CI golden hashes is a fixed 7-day period containing one DST transition, one negative-price episode, one peak-critical day, one high aFRR clearing price block, and one day with a degraded input feed.
The canonical window is a versioned artefact and changing it is a reviewed baseline update.
T1 documents the consolidated invariant register: every INV-*, its severity, where it is checked, and which level tests it.
T2 documents the property and metamorphic suite by layer and by seam.
T3 documents golden replay, the run manifest, the Merkle chain, the acyclicity audit and the bisect workflow.
T4 documents fill model calibration, quoting policy evaluation and drift alerting.
T5 documents optimality gap instrumentation and scaling curves.
T6 documents lookahead poisoning, config poisoning, contract fuzzing, ledger tampering and stale artefacts.

The compliance architecture is not a test of the simulator: L4 is external and fixed, and T4 measures how well the engine's model of the simulator matches it rather than asserting that the simulator is realistic.

The compliance architecture is not a forecasting benchmark: forecast skill is an offline concern, T2 asserts that Belief serves what it was given at the right knowledge time rather than that the forecast was good, and forecast error is measured ex post in the forecastError bucket.
No amount of property testing tells you how much money the Tier 3 heuristic costs; only T5 does.
Line coverage is reported and not gated, and the gate is the invariant register: every HALT invariant provoked by at least one test, every seam replayed, and every tier's gap measured.
